Revisiting the Factor Structure of Grit: A Commentary on Duckworth and Quinn (2009) Angela L. Duckworth1, Patrick D. Quinn2, and Eli Tsukayama3 1Psychology Department, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; 2Department of Applied Health Science, School of Public Health, Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana; 3Business Administration Division, University of Hawaii-West Oahu, Kapolei, Hawaii ABSTRACT This commentary addresses debate over the factor structure of the Grit Scale in both its original and short forms. Commonly (and in our own work), factor solutions are used to establish dimen- sionality of the construct being measured. For example, a two-factor hierarchical model was pro- posed for the Short Grit Scale. It has since been pointed out, correctly, that the specified model cannot be distinguished from a model with two correlated subfactors and no higher-order factor. In this commentary, we acknowledge the mathematical equivalence of these specifications and our error in interpretation. However, we also take the opportunity to admit a more profound cor- rection. It is now clear to us that statistical answers cannot definitively settle certain theoretical rid- dles, and our argument for grit as a compound of related but distinct dispositions should not have relied so heavily on the optimal factor solution for a questionnaire devised to assess it. Rather, a conceptual question demands a conceptual answer, which we briefly attempt here. We conclude by noting the need for improved operationalizations of the tendency to stay committed to goals for years (passion) while working assiduously toward their achievement (perseverance). ARTICLE HISTORY Received 7 October 2020 Accepted 29 May 2021 Grit was introduced by Duckworth et al. (2007) as the com- pound of passion and perseverance for long-term goals. In the context of grit, passion refers to the tendency to remain committed to the same goals over months and years, and perseverance refers to the tendency to work diligently toward those goals, even in the face of setbacks. Notably, these dual tendencies emerged in interviews with high achievers across a range of physical and intellectual domains (Duckworth et al., 2007) but had been earlier noted in stud- ies of eminence (e.g., Cox, 1926; Galton, 1869). In an effort to reduce administration time, Duckworth and Quinn (2009) eliminated four items from the original 12-item Grit Scale (Duckworth et al., 2007) to create the 8-item Grit-S Scale. The purpose of this commentary is to revisit the con- ceptualization and operationalization of grit, as well as rec- ommended applications of the Grit Scale in both its short and original forms. In the development and validation of both forms of the Grit Scale, Duckworth and colleagues proposed a hierarch- ical structure with two first-order factors for passion and perseverance. Crede (2019) has pointed out that a hierarch- ical model with two first-order factors and an equality con- straint is not mathematically distinguishable from a nonhierarchical model with two correlated first-order fac- tors. This is true, and we here acknowledge our error in interpretation. Of course, absence of evidence is not evi- dence of absence, and as Crede et al. (2017) note, “high cor- relations would suggest that a higher-order construct is plausible” (p. 493). Guo et al. (2019) recently conducted a meta-analysis on the correlation between passion and perse- verance subscales across 39 studies; their meta-analytic esti- mate of r ¼ .43 cannot be taken as evidence for or against a higher-order factor of grit. More generally, the factor structure of the Grit Scale has generated a surprisingly vigorous debate with no obvious convergence. To date, we have identified 42 articles, includ- ing 36 publications in peer-reviewed journals, proposing various dimensional structures—including a single unidi- mensional factor (e.g., Gonzalez et al., 2020; Jachimowicz et al., 2019), two correlated lower-order factors (e.g., Guo et al., 2019), a hierarchical model with a single higher-order factor comprising two lower-order factors (e.g., Jachimowicz et al., 2018), and a bifactor model (e.g., Disabato et al., 2019). Srivastava (2020) has pointed out that in the personality literature, factor analysis is frequently deployed in service of discerning the optimal number of personality factors—des- pite the fact that “there is no reason to expect that any dimension reduction of natural-language descriptions will carve nature or anything else at its joints” (p. 5). As a tool for summarizing covariance among a larger number of items into a smaller number of dimensions, Srivastava contends, factor analysis is useful. But as a statistical tool, factor ana- lysis is ill-suited to solve theoretical problems. Applied to the current question, this suggests that factor analysis cannot tell us whether it is useful to think about, and to attempt to  2021 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC CONTACT Angela L. Duckworth aduckworth@characterlab.org University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA. JOURNAL OF PERSONALITY ASSESSMENT https://doi.org/10.1080/00223891.2021.1942022

measure, the tendency for individuals to pursue long-term goals with both passion and perseverance. In our view, grit is best conceptualized as a compound of two distinct but related orientations toward long-term goals. In the motivation literature, passion and perseverance cor- respond with goal commitment and goal striving, respect- ively—complementary but independent activities that are both necessary for goal striving (Southwick et al., 2021; also see Keller et al., 2019). In her study of 301 geniuses, Cox (1926) likewise distinguished between persistence of motive and persistence of effort. Though distinct, passion and perse- verance are related, both describing dispositions toward goals that take months and years to complete. What’s more, it stands to reason that each facet of grit might encourage the other: Remaining steadfastly committed to a goal should incline one to strive diligently to achieve it, and diligent striving toward a goal could for a variety of reasons bolster one’s devotion. On the other hand, one can in theory main- tain an interest but never take action on it, just as it is pos- sible to be a very hard worker but to take up one project after another in sequence, without any discernible through line. Since the construct of grit refers to a compound of pas- sion and perseverance for long-term goals, the operationali- zation of grit should refer to both tendencies. Accordingly, the Grit Scale (in both its original and short forms) con- tains separate subscales for passion and perseverance, respectively. As with any multidimensional construct, researchers who are specifically interested in one facet of grit or the other are welcome to score the subscales separ- ately. However, when measuring the construct of grit as we have defined it, we recommend using the sum of both sub- scales. What about the aforementioned debate about factor structure? In addition to Srivastava’s compelling argument, reanalysis of Grit Scale data (from Study 2 in Duckworth & Quinn, 2009) reveals that various possible specifications for modeling covariance among items produces high corre- lations between the different specifications of grit and similar estimates of predictive validity (see Tables 1 and 2). Whether for the original 12-item scale or the 8-item Grit-S, intercorrelations for grit scored as the average of the subscales, as a single latent factor, as a latent factor of shared variance between the two subscales, or as a latent factor of shared variance among the items minus the two subscales (i.e., the general factor in a bifactor model) range from r ¼ 0.91 to 0.99 (avg. r ¼ .97) for the original 12-item scale, and r ¼ 0.96 to 1.00 (avg. r ¼ .99) for the Grit-S (see Tables 1 and 2).1 Likewise, for these diverse approaches to creating grit scores, predictive validity esti- mates for the measured outcomes of career changes and educational attainment were similar (see Tables 1 and 2). It seems fitting to close this commentary by underscoring that our early work on grit was far from perfect. For example, in Studies 2 and 5 of Duckworth and Quinn (2009), we used the phrase “more likely” when it would have been more appropriate to have used the phrase “greater odds” to describe the odds ratios that were (correctly) reported in tables summarizing binary logistic regression models. The sentence “Cadets who scored a standard devi- ation higher than average on the Grit–S were 99% more likely to complete summer training” should have been phrased as “Cadets who scored a standard deviation higher than average on the Grit–S had 99% greater odds of com- pleting summer training.” More important, it is clear in retrospect that the benefit of reducing administration time by less than a minute was not worth the cost of omitting four Grit Scale items with strong content validity—particu- larly two items specifying especially long time frames for passion (“My interests change from year to year” [reverse- scored]) and perseverance (“I have achieved a goal that took years of work”). Clifton (2020) has pointed out that it is sometimes the case that improving metrics of reliability can inadvertently result in reductions in validity. Perhaps, rather than reducing scale items, we ought to have devoted our- selves to developing an improved questionnaire in which the two-factor structure was not confounded with positively- scored (i.e., perseverance) and reverse-scored (i.e., passion) items. We note that Jachimowicz et al. (2019) have done so but, to our knowledge, have not directly compared one-fac- tor and two-factor factor solutions. Indeed, as we continue to explore the construct of grit and, in tandem, as we grow in skill and sophistication as researchers, our eagerness to improve upon past work grows. For example, we see an urgent need to relate grit to other constructs in its nomological net (e.g., harmonious and obsessive passion, self-concordant goals), to clarify its location in the Big Five personality taxonomy, and to iden- tify contextual factors that give rise to within-person vari- ation (see Southwick et al., 2021). Compared to our development of the original Grit Scale and its short form over a decade ago, these alternative measures will, we hope, more closely adhere to contemporary best practices in scale development (Clark & Watson, 2019). Indeed, we anticipate that with each advance, the limitations of prior research will become more salient—signaling, in our view, forward progress rather than the lack thereof.
